comparison.summary: Five JavaScript approaches are available here. The first uses binary search with exact sequence IDs, giving expected O(n log n) time and O(n log n) space. The rolling-hash solution verifies actual elements, and the three suffix solutions remain available.
details: The exact-ID version builds power-of-two block levels by assigning a distinct ID to each ordered pair of half IDs. It then identifies each tested window with its first and last block IDs, whose blocks cover the whole sequence. It takes O(n log n) expected time with expected constant-time Map operations and O(n log n) space, where n is the number of elements. No rolling-hash collision checks or repeated element comparisons are needed.

The rolling-hash version binary-searches the length and groups windows by hash, then compares their actual elements before combining occurrence counts. It takes O(n log n + C) time with expected constant-time Map operations, where C counts all exact element comparisons, and O(n) space. A conservative worst-case time bound is O(n³ log n).
The simple suffix version copies and sorts whole suffixes, then compares neighboring suffixes directly. It is exact, but takes O(n² log n) time with O(n log n) sort comparisons and O(n²) space.

The optimized suffix array version uses rank doubling and stable counting sort, then Kasai’s algorithm for adjacent LCP values. It applies the same unique-prefix formula in O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
The suffix automaton propagates occurrence counts through the shorterId tree and finds the shortest length represented by a node that occurs once. It takes O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

The older Python solution binary-searches the length and counts rolling hashes without checking the actual elements, taking O(n log n) time and O(n) space. That hash-only comparison is incorrect for nums = [1,20,2,1,20,2]: it returns 3 instead of 2. With base 19, [1,20] and [2,1] both hash to 39, hiding the unique pair [2,1]. All five saved JavaScript solutions return the correct answer 2.

Choosing a base larger than the values prevents that base-19 example from colliding, but modular collisions can still happen. The saved rolling-hash version keeps separate exact-window groups under the same hash; the first solution instead uses exact sequence IDs throughout.

solutions.title: Binary search + exact sequence IDs
solutions.approach: First assign exact IDs to every block whose length is a power of two. Single-value blocks use the values themselves as IDs. At each later level, give each distinct ordered pair of left-half and right-half IDs its own new ID, reusing it whenever both halves match. Then binary-search the smallest length that has a unique window. For each candidate length, choose the largest power-of-two block that fits and identify every window by its first-block and last-block IDs. Those two blocks cover the entire window, so matching both IDs means the complete sequences are equal. Count the pairs; if any appears once, search shorter lengths, otherwise search longer lengths.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n) expected, assuming expected constant-time Map operations
notes: IDs are exact labels assigned to ordered pairs, not rolling hashes. IDs are local to one block level, and 0 is a valid ID, so the code uses .has() to test whether a pair already has an ID.
The first and last blocks may overlap. When the window length is already a power of two, they are the same block; the window is still counted once.
Precomputing all block levels uses O(n log n) space. The rolling-hash, optimized suffix array, and suffix automaton alternatives below use O(n) space.

#### 1. Input and the result we want

Use `nums = [1, 2, 1, 2, 1]`, so `n = nums.length = 5`. We want the shortest continuous subarray that appears **exactly once**. Occurrences at different starting indices count separately, even when they overlap.

| Index | Value |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 1 |
| 3 | 2 |
| 4 | 1 |

The code first gives exact IDs to blocks of lengths `1`, `2`, and `4`. It then binary-searches a candidate length. A window of that length is identified by the ordered pair `(first block ID, last block ID)`. Counting those pairs counts identical windows exactly.

#### 2. What an exact ID means

An ID is a label for a sequence at one particular block length. At level `0`, each block contains one number, so the number itself is its exact ID: value `1` has ID `1`, and value `2` has ID `2`. Initialize `idsByLevel = [nums]`; no copy or separate scan of the values is needed for this assignment.

```text
level 0, block length 1: [1, 2, 1, 2, 1]
```

At each later level, split a block into equal left and right halves. Look up their ordered pair `(leftId, rightId)` in nested Maps. Give a new pair the next unused ID; reuse the existing ID when both halves match. Order matters: `(1, 2)` and `(2, 1)` are different pairs.

The first Map key is the left ID; its value is another Map keyed by the right ID. In a snapshot such as `1 → Map { 2 → 0 }`, left ID `1` and right ID `2` together map to sequence ID `0`. The two keys are stored separately, so there is no numeric hash or combined-key formula to collide.

IDs are local to their level. For example, ID `0` at level `1` will mean `[1, 2]`, while ID `0` at level `2` will mean `[1, 2, 1, 2]`. The code always compares IDs from the same level. Each new level gets a fresh Map and resets `nextId` to `0`.

#### 5. Why these IDs and two blocks identify the exact sequence

**Exact IDs at each level.** At level `0`, IDs match exactly when the single values match. Assume that is true at the previous level. At the next level, two longer blocks get the same ID exactly when both their left-half IDs and their right-half IDs match. By the assumption, their actual left halves and actual right halves match, so the entire blocks match. Different pairs get different IDs because `nextId` increases after every new pair. This proves exactness level by level.

**Cover an arbitrary length.** Let `L` mean the candidate window length and `B` mean the largest power of two at most `L`. Then `B <= L < 2 × B`. Take the first `B` elements and the last `B` elements. Their combined coverage reaches every position in the window; they overlap by `2 × B - L` elements. There is no uncovered middle.

For length `3`, `B = 2`. In the first window `[1, 2, 1]`, the first block `[1, 2]` covers indices `0, 1`, and the last block `[2, 1]` covers indices `1, 2`. Index `1` is covered twice. The overlap is intentional. If both exact block IDs match another window, all positions match, including the overlap.

When `L = B`, the first and last blocks are the same whole window. Its pair contains the same ID twice, such as `(0, 0)`. The loop still records that window **once**, with a single count update.

**Why binary search is valid.** A unique window of length less than `n` can be extended right if there is a following element. If it touches the right edge, its length is less than `n`, so there must be a preceding element; extend it left. If the extended window occurred twice, the original window would occur twice at the same offset inside it, which is a contradiction. Therefore every length above a successful length also succeeds. The whole array occurs once, so length `n` is a valid initial answer.

solutions.title: Binary search + rolling hash
solutions.approach: Binary-search the smallest length for which some continuous subarray occurs exactly once. For each tested length, build the first window’s polynomial hash, then slide by removing the outgoing value’s weighted contribution, shifting the remaining weights, and adding the incoming value. Store a list of representative windows and occurrence counts under each hash. When hashes match, compare the actual elements before increasing a count; different sequences keep separate groups. After recording every window, a group with count 1 means this length works, so search shorter lengths. Otherwise, search longer lengths. A unique window can always be extended while remaining unique, which makes binary search valid.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n + C) with expected constant-time Map operations; O(n³ log n) conservative worst case

variables.C: Total element comparisons in sameWindow across all tested lengths, including comparisons between matching duplicate windows and between different windows that share a hash.

notes: Equal hashes are only a reason to compare two windows, not proof that they are equal. Exact element checks keep this version correct even when different windows share a hash.
Large inputs with many repeated windows can make exact comparisons expensive. The optimized suffix array and suffix automaton solutions below offer stronger performance bounds.

| 2 | 1 |

| 4 | 1 |

A window is one subarray of the length currently being tested. `start` is its first index. `hasUnique(length)` returns whether **any** window of that length occurs once; it does not require every window to be unique.

#### 2. Scan the values and choose the base

Multiplying by `BASE` shifts the existing values one position to the left in the hash. For `[a, b, c]`, the hash before taking the remainder is `a × BASE² + b × BASE + c`. Because the window is shorter than `n`, an element exists to its left in that case. If that longer window occurred twice, the original window would also occur twice at the same position inside those two occurrences. That contradicts the original window being unique. #### 8. A collision example: one length-2 check

- `[1, 9994]`: `1 × 100001 + 9994 = 109995`; `109995 % 1000000007 = 109995`.

- `[10001, 1]`: `10001 × 100001 + 1 = 1000110002`; `1000110002 % 1000000007 = 109995`.

#### 9. Time, space, and what the extra comparisons cost

Let `n` be the number of elements and `C` be the total number of element comparisons performed by `sameWindow` across **all tested lengths**. `C` includes comparisons between truly identical windows as well as comparisons caused by accidental hash collisions. The main example performs `3 + 3 + 4 = 10` such comparisons.

The maximum scan costs `O(n)`. Hash construction, sliding, and creating or updating at most one group per window cost `O(n)` per check, assuming expected constant-time Map operations. Every candidate group visited during the bucket search performs at least one element comparison, so that search overhead is covered by `C`. Binary search tests `O(log n)` lengths, so total time is **`O(n log n + C)`**. A conservative worst-case bound is **`O(n³ log n)`**: a check can compare `O(n²)` pairs of windows and inspect up to `O(n)` elements per pair.

Space is **`O(n)`**: one check stores at most one group per window, using a start index and a count. It does not copy subarrays. The next check creates a fresh Map, and the old one is no longer needed.

Exact comparisons can be expensive on large inputs with many repeated windows. The optimized suffix array and suffix automaton solutions below avoid this repeated element-by-element verification.

solutions.title: Simple suffix sorting + LCP
solutions.approach: Copy every suffix and sort those arrays lexicographically. For each suffix, compare its elements with the previous and next suffix to find their longest common prefixes (LCP). A unique prefix needs max(previous LCP, next LCP) + 1 elements; take the smallest such length that fits inside its suffix.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n² log n) with O(n log n) sort comparisons
notes: This version makes the steps easier to follow, but copies n(n + 1) / 2 elements. Use an optimized version for large inputs such as 100,000 numbers.

solutions.title: Optimized suffix array + LCP
solutions.approach: Sort suffix starting indices without copying the suffixes: rank doubling compares increasingly long prefixes using stable counting sorts. Kasai’s algorithm calculates neighboring LCP values while reusing matches from the previous suffix. For each suffix, compute max(previous LCP, next LCP) + 1 and take the smallest length that fits inside that suffix.
notes: This optimized version uses the separate function name smallestUniqueSubarraySuffixArray.

solutions.title: Suffix automaton
solutions.approach: Build a suffix automaton that groups subarrays sharing the same ending positions. Add each node’s occurrence count to its shorterId parent after processing its children. For a node seen exactly once, nodes[shorterId].maxLength + 1 is its shortest unique length; take the minimum of those lengths.
notes: Preserved naming: currNum, newId, lastId, shorterId, nextId, cloneId, ROOT_ID, and NO_ID. Transitions remain plain JavaScript objects.
